newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE-Alfa Romeo plans for its renaissance.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Alfa Romeo plans for its renaissance.

text.p: Alfa Romeo's renaissance has been a long time coming. Bedevilled by poor quality and held back by former state ownership, Italy's famous sporty car company has remained in the doldrums for decades.

For Alfa's owners of the last 10 years, giant carmaker Fiat, all is set to change. But never has so much depended on one model, planned for launch this autumn, to break the stranglehold of German cars on the sporty executive car sector.
Fiat has been hard at work spending five trillion lire ($3 billion) on Alfa to try to revive its former glories, when it dominated on the race track in the 1940s and 1950s.

But as Fiat has pumped money in, sales of Alfas worldwide have slipped over the last few years as it struggled to overcome quality problems at its southern Italian car plant and make inroads into a tough northern European prestige car market.

Alfa is pinning its hopes on a new sporty executive car, the 156, which it forecasts will more than double peak sales of the outgoing ageing 155 and get close to sales of the sector's front runner and benchmark car, the BMW 3-series.
It's a very tall order. So Alfa has spent a lot of time applying the finishing touches to this new medium-large car to give it an Italian flair, and with it rests Alfa's future.
"We are ambitious for the 156, and we see it doing well in new markets for us," Giuseppe Perlo, senior vice president for product at Fiat Auto, told Reuters in Fiat's home town Turin.
TURBULENT HISTORY FOR FAMOUS CAR MARQUE

Alfa -- or Anonima Lombarda Fabbrica di Automobili -- was formed in 1910 in central Milan with the firm's trade mark chosen with a Milanese flavour as a red cross and the Visconti snake, from one of Milan's most famous historical families.

Neopolitan entrepreneur Nicola Romeo soon took over the company and his name became inextricably linked to the group's fortunes. However, the combined group soon ran into financial problems and was rescued by the Italian state in the 1930s.

Under state-ownership, the firm enjoyed its best years on the race track after World War Two, and its entry into the mass market with its much-loved Giulietta range was rated a great success in the 1950s.

Alfa's problems mounted in the late 1960s with over-ambitious plans for expansion linked to political and social difficulties in Italy, which led to a label of poor quality at Alfa that the company has sought ever since to combat.
A second factory was built at Pomigliano D'Arco, near Naples, in the late 1960s to build a new model, the Alfasud, while the Milan factory closed and moved to Arese, just outside the city, in 1975.

The first cars rolled out of Pomigliano in 1971 with the Milano logo dropped from the Alfa Romeo badge for the first time. The over ambitious expansion at Pomigliani allied to labour difficulties led to some commentators dubbing Pomigliano as the "worst car factory in western Europe".

The Italian state soon tired of the drain on cash at the loss-making company producing around 220,000 cars a year, and in 1987 Fiat stepped in, after U.S. car giant Ford had put in an offer, and so brought Italy's three major car marques Fiat, Lancia and Alfa all under the same roof.
FIAT STRUGGLES WITH ALFA'S PROBLEMS
Fiat also met trouble after the takeover, as a string of new models failed to stop output halving to an annual production of just over 100,000 by 1994.

Alfa's production director Giorgio Pavia explained that sales had been weak over the last five years due a poor Italian market, the relatively unsuccessful medium-large 155 and the fall in sales of the ageing 164, the biggest model in the Alfa range.

Fiat's renewal programme after its 1987 takeover saw the Alfa 164 rolled out at the end of that year, the 155 in 1992, the small-medium car range 145/166 at the end of 1994, and then the specialist sports models GTV and Spider in 1995.

The 145/146s were upgraded last year to incorporate Alfa's unique twin-spark engines and these two models now account for nearly two-thirds of Alfa's European sales. But it will be the new 156 waiting in the wings that remains critical for Alfa.

In a highly competitive medium/large upmarket car sector, Alfa hopes the new 156 will sell 86,000 units in 1998 and stabilise at around 121,000 in 1999 and beyond, pushing total Alfa annual sales back above 200,000.

But there is a lot of tough competition especially from BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen's upmarket Audi. The old 155 at its best only reached a peak of 45,000-50,000 sales a year and sold just over 21,000 in Europe last year, and Alfa has never done well in northern Europe.
Still Alfa's Perlo is upbeat. "We will have two new models in the next few months and then the whole range will have been replaced between October 1994 and the middle of 1998."
Alfa worldwide sales reached 131,000 in 1996. Clearly, to push back to the 200,000 level it needs a successful 156 and also a popular new 164, due for launch early next year.
DESIGNERS GO FOR LATIN FLAIR

Designers have tried to add a certain Latin flair with the 156. The traditional Alfa shield in the radiator is cut deep into the front bumper harking back to the 1950s Giulietta, pushing the registration plate to one side in an American style.
Front door handles revive 1960s chrome, while the rear door handles are hidden in the black plastic surrounds of the rear windows to give the appearance of a two-door coupe to this four-door car.
Perlo says Fiat has worked hard at Pomigliano over the last two years improving quality with the 145/146, and the 156 will be of a similar high quality.

Still the obstacles loom large -- BMW brings out its new 3-series at the end of the year and Audi has been aggressive in this market with its A4 model. Alfa has no plans to return to the U.S. and, with still around half of all Alfas sold in Italy, it could struggle to compete in northern Europe.
Fiat's top executives privately admit the 156 is crucial to Alfa's success.
Only time will tell.
